title: Self-Neglect and Hoarding Procedure
summary: How we recognise and respond when a person we support neglects their own hygiene, health or home, or hoards until their home becomes unsafe: what care workers do and report at the visit, how assessors rate clutter and risk, how we work with the person at their pace within the Mental Capacity Act, when we refer to the local authority and community partners, and how we keep staff safe in cluttered or unsanitary homes. For all staff.

keyPoints.intro: Self-neglect and hoarding build up slowly, and you may be the only person who sees inside the home. This is what you do at every visit when you notice it.
points: If the person is in danger now (very cold, seriously unwell, unable to reach food, drink or the toilet, or at risk from fire or gas), call 999 where needed and phone the office or On-call Manager, from outside if the home is unsafe.

Before you leave the visit, phone the office (On-call Manager out of hours) and speak to a person about any new or worsening sign, such as poor hygiene, little food, rubbish, soiling, clutter building up, pests or refused help.

Tell them straight away if an exit or your route is blocked, clutter is near heat or smoking materials, there is no working smoke alarm, heating, water or food, or essential care or medicines are declined.

If neither the office nor the On-call Manager answers within 15 minutes, phone the Registered Manager or Deputy Manager directly. If you call 999, stay until help arrives or the office says you may leave.

Never throw away, move or tidy a person's belongings, food or papers, even if they look like rubbish, unless they agree at that visit and the visit plan includes the task; never take waste or belongings out of the home.
Follow the agreed steps in the visit plan at the person's pace, never criticise them or their home, and never agree new tasks yourself: ask the office.
A choice you think unwise does not mean the person lacks capacity. Write what they say and do in their own words, and tell the office the same day if you doubt they understand the risks.

Write factual, respectful daily visit notes before you check out, describing what you saw and what was declined; never photograph the home or belongings; body map photographs follow the Consent to Care Policy.

Wear the gloves and apron the risk assessment sets; where pests are recorded, do not sit on beds or soft furniture; never touch unknown substances or pest baits; handle found needles only as the Sharps Safety and Needlestick Injury Procedure says.
If you cannot get in, move around or use equipment safely, do not force it: give only the care that is safe and phone the office, who will decide what happens to the visit.

Self-neglect and hoarding are covered in your induction and annual safeguarding refresher; at spot checks you will be asked about the agreed steps and controls for people with a self-neglect support plan.

blocks.p: {{organisation}} supports people who stop looking after their own hygiene, health or home, or keep possessions until their home becomes unsafe; our care workers are often the first to see this. We respect each person's right to live as they choose and never treat a way of living we would not choose as a lack of capacity. Equally, we do not stand by while a person comes to serious harm because of needs they cannot manage alone.

{{organisation}} never clears out or disposes of a person's belongings against their wishes, and never reduces or withdraws care because of the condition of a home without a recorded decision by the Registered Manager.

bullets: Signs are recognised early, reported the same day and recorded factually.
Every concern is assessed in the home, with clutter and risk rated consistently.
The person's views, choices and capacity guide what happens.
Risk is reduced through an agreed support plan, community partners and, where the conditions are met, a safeguarding referral.
Staff stay safe in cluttered or unsanitary homes.

blocks.p: This procedure applies to everyone who works for us, at visits, in the office and on call. It covers every adult we support who neglects their own personal care, health or surroundings, including hoarding of objects, food, medicines or animals. Where another household member causes the conditions and they affect the person we support, we use the same assessment and the safeguarding lead decides whether it is neglect by others.

Neglect or abuse by anyone else follows the Safeguarding Concerns: Reporting, Referral and Enquiry Procedure; clutter as a fire risk, the Fire Safety in People's Homes Policy; declined visits and tasks, the Visit Cancellations and Refusals of Care Procedure; capable people's risky choices, the Positive Risk-Taking Policy; and a visit where nobody answers, the No Reply, No Access and Missing Person Procedure.

rows: Self-neglect
Neglecting to care for one's own personal hygiene, health or surroundings, including behaviour such as hoarding (Care and support statutory guidance, chapter 14).
Hoarding
Acquiring and keeping many items, or animals, and having great difficulty parting with them, so that rooms cannot be used for their purpose or become unsafe.
Clutter Image Rating

A nine-picture scale for the living room, kitchen and bedroom, from 1 (no clutter) to 9 (most severe). The assessor records the picture closest to each room, rating other rooms against the nearest equivalent. Level 4 or above in any room is our clutter threshold, as in the Fire Safety in People's Homes Policy.
Say/do gap
A person can explain how they would keep safe but repeatedly cannot carry it out. It is evidence for a capacity assessment, never proof that the person lacks capacity.
Self-neglect support plan
The agreed steps, who does what, staff controls and review date, recorded in the Risks part of the care plan and the visit plans, with the person's own words about what they want.
Multi-agency risk management meeting
A meeting the local authority convenes under the local Safeguarding Adults Board's procedures (local names vary) to agree a shared plan where risk is high.

blocks.p: The Directors provide the assessors and visit time this procedure needs. The Nominated Individual reviews self-neglect figures in the safeguarding reports and must agree in writing before any package is handed back for a person with an open self-neglect record.

The Registered Manager, or the Deputy Manager in their absence, makes the route and referral decisions, approves High risk controls and best interests decisions, decides any change to how visits are delivered, requests and attends multi-agency meetings, and applies each area's Safeguarding Adults Board self-neglect procedures, linked from the Local Safeguarding Contacts sheet.

subsections.heading: Care Coordinators and Field Care Supervisors

blocks.p: Care Coordinators record reported concerns, arrange assessments, keep the chronology, make partner referrals, brief care workers before their next visit whenever the plan changes, and keep review dates. Field Care Supervisors, and Care Coordinators authorised as assessors, carry out self-neglect assessments and reviews in the home and check at spot checks that the support plan is followed.

Out of hours, the On-call Manager takes reports, decides immediate safety actions, makes emergency referrals and hands over to the Registered Manager or Deputy Manager by 10am on the next working day.

subsections.heading: Care Workers, Senior Care Workers and Office staff

blocks.p: Care Workers and Senior Care Workers recognise and report signs, record factually and follow the support plan exactly. Office staff pass every phoned report to the Care Coordinator the same working day, and at once to the safeguarding lead if it includes an urgent sign.

rows: Personal care and health

Very poor hygiene; the same soiled clothes for days; untreated wounds, sores, infections or pressure damage; weight loss or dehydration; missed appointments; medicines stockpiled, unused or hidden; bought medicines running out fast.
Food and daily living
Little or no food; mouldy or out-of-date food; no heating, lighting, hot water or working toilet; disconnection notices or unopened post piling up.
The home
Rubbish, soiled linen or human or animal waste building up; strong odours; rats, mice, cockroaches, bed bugs or fleas; damp, mould or disrepair the person will not let anyone fix.
Hoarding

Rooms that cannot be used for their purpose; blocked doors, stairs or windows; narrow paths; items stacked high or near heaters, the cooker or smoking materials; sleeping in a chair because the bed is covered; more animals than the person can care for.
Engagement
Declining essential care, equipment or health appointments; refusing to let professionals or repairers in; growing isolation; distress or anger when belongings are touched.

blocks.p: Causes include dementia, depression, psychosis, hoarding disorder, brain injury, physical illness, pain, medicines side effects, alcohol or drug use, bereavement and trauma; sometimes none is found. A sudden change in someone who managed well before suggests a health cause, so the Care Coordinator asks the GP to review the person the same working day.

sections.heading: What care workers do at the visit

steps: If anyone is in danger now (fire, smoke, smell of gas, a collapsing ceiling or pile, serious illness or injury, the person very cold with no heating, or unable to reach food, drink or the toilet), call 999 where needed and phone the office or On-call Manager. If the home is unsafe, get out or stay out and phone from outside. Stay until help arrives or the office says you may leave, however long past the planned end of the visit.

Give the care in the visit plan, essential tasks first. If clutter stops a task being done safely, for example the hoist cannot be positioned or the route to the bathroom is blocked, give only the care that is safe and phone the office before you leave; the office arranges the care still due.

Ask before you touch anything. Never throw away, move or tidy belongings, food or papers unless the person agrees at that visit and the visit plan includes the task. Never agree new tasks yourself; pass requests to the office. Never take waste or belongings out of the home (Waste Management in People's Homes Procedure).
With the person's agreement, keep clear the route you need, and never climb over or lean on piles.

Before you leave the visit, phone the office or On-call Manager and speak to a person about any new or worsening sign in Recognising self-neglect and hoarding. Tell them straight away if any of these urgent signs is present: an exit or your route is blocked; clutter is near a heater, cooker or smoking materials; there is no working smoke alarm, heating, water, lighting or toilet; there is no food in the home; essential care, food, drink or medicines are declined and the person may be at risk; there are signs of serious illness, infection, injury or pressure damage; pests are in the bed or food areas; you find needles or unknown substances; an animal is in distress; the person has changed suddenly; or someone else may be neglecting or exploiting them. Phone from outside if you feel unsafe; if nobody answers within 15 minutes, phone the Registered Manager or Deputy Manager directly.
A sign the person's self-neglect support plan already covers, and which has not got worse, is recorded in the daily visit notes without a call and considered at the next review.

Before you check out, write factual, respectful daily visit notes: what you saw and smelt, what the person said in their own words, what you did and what was declined. Write 'papers and boxes cover the sofa and floor; the path from the front door to the kitchen is about 40cm wide', not 'the house is a tip'. Where someone else may be responsible, write only that a concern has been reported.
Never photograph the home or belongings, or any injury as evidence; describe conditions in words. Body map photographs for skin or wound monitoring follow the Consent to Care Policy.

blocks.p: Signs found at an initial assessment or care plan review are assessed at that visit or within 5 days. Reports from relatives, neighbours, landlords or other professionals, and concerns passed on under other procedures are handled like reports from our staff.

The assessor arranges the visit with the person, explains why they are coming and enters a room only with their agreement. The assessment is recorded on the day in the risk assessments and safeguarding record, counts as the focused review the Care Plan Review Procedure requires after a safeguarding concern, and covers:

bullets: the person's own account: how they see their home and health, what matters to them, their history, what they would like to change, if anything, and who they trust;

the dated Clutter Image Rating for each room the person uses, in the home environment risk assessment, which is reviewed for access and escape routes, trips and falls, unstable piles, space for equipment, utilities, sanitation, pests, damp, sharps and animals;

fire: clutter at level 4 or above in any room, or a blocked escape route, means an individual fire risk assessment within 7 days and a fire and rescue service referral (see the partner table); level 7 or above in any room counts as a blocked escape route unless the assessor records why not;
care needs: hygiene, skin, continence, nutrition, hydration and medicines, with any stockpiled medicines reported to the GP the same day;
any reason to doubt the person's capacity for the specific decisions involved, including a say/do gap;
possible causes, professionals already involved, and risks to others, such as children in the household, neighbours in a shared building or our staff.

blocks.p: If the person declines the assessment visit, the assessor completes it from care workers' observations and the daily visit notes, offers another visit at a time the person chooses, and tells the Registered Manager. Each risk is rated with the likelihood and severity method in the Risk Assessment and Home Environment Risk Assessment Procedure, and the highest residual risk sets the response.

rows: Low
Agreed approach recorded in the care plan; care workers report any change.
At every care plan review
Medium
Self-neglect support plan agreed with the person within 7 days of the report; with consent, the GP and other partners contacted within 5 working days.
Every 4 weeks by the Care Coordinator or Field Care Supervisor, in the home at least every other time
High

As Medium, plus staff controls approved by the Registered Manager or Deputy Manager before the task, shown in My care at a glance and briefed to every allocated worker before their next visit; the safeguarding lead decides on a referral the same working day; no worker in their first 4 weeks of lone working visits alone.
Every 2 weeks
Very high

The task or visit does not go ahead as planned; the assessor phones the Registered Manager or Deputy Manager (On-call Manager out of hours) at once; a safe alternative is decided the same day and the person still receives essential care; only the Registered Manager approves a return to the planned visit; the safeguarding lead decides on a referral at once.
Weekly until the risk falls

blocks.p: We presume the person has capacity. A decision others think unwise does not show a lack of capacity, but repeated unwise decisions that put the person at significant risk are a reason to look more closely. Capacity is assessed for a specific decision when it needs to be made, such as accepting help to wash or agreeing a clear route, under the Mental Capacity Act and Best Interests Policy.

bullets: A capacity doubt is reported the same day and assessed by an authorised assessor within 7 days. A say/do gap is evidenced on at least two occasions and from the daily visit notes, and discussed with the person.

Where the person has capacity, their decision is respected: the risks discussed are recorded within 2 working days under the Positive Risk-Taking Policy and help is offered again at every review. Where part of the care plan is declined, the Registered Manager decides within 1 working day whether the rest can be given safely and tells the commissioner in writing.

Where the person lacks capacity for a decision about our care, a best interests decision is approved by the Registered Manager or Deputy Manager before use, with a best interests meeting where those consulted disagree or a restriction is involved.

Clearing the home, disposing of possessions, moving home and tenancy matters are not our decisions: the Care Coordinator writes within 2 working days to the commissioner (for a self-funder, the local authority) with our observations and the person's views. For medical treatment, the Care Coordinator gives the treating professional our observations the same day and asks them to consider capacity. A verified attorney or deputy decides within their authority.
Pressure from another person is not a lack of capacity; it is reported as a safeguarding concern.

blocks.p: Change is usually slow, and good risk management may be the best achievable outcome. We:

bullets: keep the core care team stable, introducing any new member on a joint visit where the self-neglect risk is Medium or higher;

start from what matters to the person and agree one small, specific step at a time, such as a clear path from bed to toilet or one worktop for preparing food, with a target date set with them and recorded in their words;
never carry out or arrange a 'blitz' clean-up; a larger clearance is planned with the person, at their pace, by a specialist service they or their representative choose;
respect what items mean to the person, say 'belongings', never 'junk', and keep offering help: a refusal today is not a refusal for ever;

offer practical help with consent: GP review and, through the GP, mental health or drug and alcohol services; hoarding support groups; the council's bulky waste collection, booked by the person or family; benefits advice; and utility priority services registers;
expect setbacks: a relapse leads to a review, never to blame.

blocks.p: Family and informal carers are involved as far as the person agrees, and their roles are recorded in the People involved part and the care plan. A relative clearing belongings against the person's wishes, or without lawful authority where the person lacks capacity, is reported the same day; the Care Coordinator speaks to the family within 2 working days and the safeguarding lead decides whether it is a safeguarding concern.

The statutory guidance says self-neglect may not lead to a section 42 enquiry: it is decided case by case, depending on the person's ability to protect themselves by controlling their own behaviour. The safeguarding lead refers to the local authority when the person appears to have care and support needs and, because of them, appears unable to protect themselves, and any of these applies:

bullets: a risk to life or of serious harm (severity 4 or 5) to the person;
clutter at level 7 or above in any room, or a High or Very high fire risk;
essential care, treatment or services refused, leaving the person at serious risk;
a risk to others, including children, neighbours or our staff, that we cannot control;
the person lacks capacity for the relevant decisions and our best interests approach has not reduced the risk;
a High risk not falling after 4 weeks of the support plan, or a Medium risk rising at two reviews in a row.

blocks.p: The referral follows the Safeguarding Concerns: Reporting, Referral and Enquiry Procedure and any local self-neglect protocol. Our policy is that the Registered Manager (the Deputy Manager in their absence) notifies CQC of every self-neglect safeguarding referral within 24 hours of the referral under the Statutory Notifications to CQC Procedure, whether or not regulation 18 of the Care Quality Commission (Registration) Regulations 2009 requires it. Where the local authority makes no enquiry but the risk stays High or Very high, or the person declines a referral, the Registered Manager writes within 2 working days asking for a multi-agency risk management meeting. Wherever needs have changed, the Care Coordinator asks in writing within 2 working days for a needs assessment or review: the local authority must assess, even if the person refuses, where they are experiencing or at risk of abuse or neglect (Care Act 2014, section 11(2)(b)), and the statutory guidance lists self-neglect among the types of abuse and neglect.

rows: GP
Suspected health cause, sudden change, untreated condition, stockpiled or overused medicines, essential care declined (the district nurse instead for wounds they treat)
Care Coordinator: the same working day for a sudden change, untreated condition or stockpiled or overused medicines; otherwise within 5 working days, with consent
Fire and rescue service
Clutter at level 4 or above in any room, a blocked exit, clutter near heat or smoking materials, a High or Very high fire risk
Care Coordinator: within 5 working days of the rating where level 4 or above is the only one of these; otherwise the same working day (Fire Safety in People's Homes Policy)
Landlord or housing provider
Repairs, pests, tenancy at risk
Care Coordinator, with consent, within 5 working days; the same working day for pests or danger
Environmental health
Pests or filthy conditions harmful to health that the person will not address; the council can require cleansing (Public Health Act 1936, section 83)
Registered Manager decides within 2 working days whether to refer, sharing without consent only under the Safeguarding Adults Policy rules
Family or local authority
Disconnection, or no heating, water or electricity
Care Coordinator, the same working day
Family, vet, animal welfare charity or RSPCA
More animals than the person can care for, fouling building up, or an animal suffering

Care Coordinator speaks to the person or family within 2 working days (the same day if an animal is suffering now); the Registered Manager decides on an RSPCA report, as the Animals and Pets in People's Homes Guideline sets out

blocks.p: The Registered Manager or Deputy Manager attends every multi-agency meeting we are invited to, with a written chronology. Our actions go into the care plan with an owner and deadline within 2 working days, and the local authority is told within 1 working day if we cannot deliver one.

rows: Narrow routes, unstable piles, trip hazards
Agreed route kept clear with the person's agreement; equipment such as a hoist used only where the space the risk assessment sets is clear.
Bed bugs, fleas, rodents or cockroaches

Apron and gloves for all care; do not sit on beds or soft furniture; coat and bag left in the car, or sealed in a plastic bag by the door if you came without one; kit box on a clean hard surface, never the floor; check clothing on leaving; uniform washed at the end of the shift at the hottest temperature it allows, at least 60°C. Staff never use pesticides or pest baits.
Human or animal waste, soiled linen, rotting food

Gloves and apron; Type IIR mask and eye protection where splashing is possible; spills cleaned as the Laundry, Soiled Linen and Spillages Procedure sets out; anything beyond the care plan task phoned to the office.
Found needles
Picked up only into a sharps container already in the home, otherwise left untouched and phoned in, as the Sharps Safety and Needlestick Injury Procedure sets out.
Unknown substances, pest baits, extensive mould
Never touched or moved (Hazardous Substances (COSHH) Procedure).
No running water
Detergent hand wipes then hand rub; only food tasks needing no handling; phoned before leaving.
Strong odours or ammonia
Ventilate with the person's agreement; if breathing is affected, leave and phone the office.

blocks.p: Workers who are pregnant, gave birth in the last 6 months, are breastfeeding or have weakened immunity are not allocated to homes where human or animal waste or pests are recorded until their individual risk assessment allows it. Any worker may refuse unsafe work in good faith under the Health and Safety Policy.

Only the Registered Manager or Deputy Manager (the On-call Manager out of hours, until handover) decides to change how visits are delivered because of conditions in the home, for example a second worker, a longer visit, a different time or care in the usable room; the person always receives essential care. The commissioner is told the same working day where commissioned care changes; if the matter is unresolved, the Registered Manager writes to the person and commissioner within 5 working days. A package is handed back only with the Nominated Individual's written agreement, after a referral decision and a multi-agency meeting held or requested, with the commissioner's agreement and within the contract notice period.

When a person with a self-neglect support plan is admitted to hospital, the Care Coordinator tells the ward or discharge team the same working day, with consent or under the Safeguarding Adults Policy sharing rules, about home conditions that affect a safe discharge. Before care restarts, the assessor checks that the route and space needed for care are usable, under the Hospital Admission and Discharge Procedure. Nobody from {{organisation}} moves or removes belongings while the person is away.

The safeguarding record holds each report, the route decision with reasons, referrals, meetings, outcomes and the Care Coordinator's chronology of key events, offers, refusals and professional contacts, updated at every review. Capacity and best interests records are kept in the Consent and decisions part of the care plan. Injuries, pests and hazards are also logged in the incident log.

Only the Registered Manager or Deputy Manager closes a self-neglect safeguarding record: when the residual risk has been Low, or Medium and stable, at two reviews in a row, the person's views are recorded and the closure conditions in the Safeguarding Concerns: Reporting, Referral and Enquiry Procedure are met. A record where a capable person declined a referral stays open for at least three months, with the Field Care Supervisor's private follow-up every 4 weeks under that procedure. Records are kept under the Records Management and Retention Policy.

blocks.p: Each new assessor's first two self-neglect assessments are checked by the Registered Manager or Deputy Manager before the route decision. At every spot check in the home of a person with a self-neglect support plan, the Field Care Supervisor asks the care worker what the agreed steps and controls are; a worker who cannot say is briefed before their next visit there. Training is recorded in training and compliance records, and staff acknowledge this procedure in CareFlow by the deadline in the Induction and Care Certificate Procedure and within 14 days of each new major version.

blocks.p: This procedure is reviewed every 12 months by the Registered Manager and approved by the Directors under the Policy Management and Document Control Policy, and sooner after a change in law, statutory guidance or local Safeguarding Adults Board procedures, a Safeguarding Adults Review involving self-neglect in our areas, a serious incident, an inspection finding, or when monitoring shows the arrangements are not working.
